name: Cathoidermie machine

card.summary: A salon galvanic (direct-current) device whose negative electrode loosens oily plugs for a clearer-looking complexion.
card.aka: Cathiodermie, galvanic facial machine, desincrustation machine, ionization device
card.note: Avoid on inflamed or sensitive skin per salon-supply guidance.

quick.overview:
The cathoidermie (cathiodermie) machine is a salon device that passes a low direct current through the skin. At the negative electrode, the current produces an alkaline solution that softens keratin and oils, a process called desincrustation, aimed at loosening blackheads and congestion.

The visible payoff is cleaner-looking pores and a smoother complexion after extraction. The technique is traditional in beauty-salon training; clinical trials of it are scarce.
quick.how: A technician applies a conductive solution and moves the negative electrode over the face for about 10 to 15 minutes at a low current, often followed by the positive electrode to introduce water-soluble products by iontophoresis. It is usually part of a facial, with extractions afterward.
quick.risks: Salon-supply guidance advises against desincrustation on inflamed acne, couperose skin or active pustules. Users may feel tingling; metal contact and electrical devices require trained handling, and people with implanted medical devices are generally advised to avoid electrotherapy.

lead: A cathoidermie machine, usually spelled cathiodermie in French salon practice, is an esthetic galvanic device. It converts mains power to a low direct current for desincrustation, a treatment developed in France in the early 1930s by Societe P.A.B. to remove what developers described as microscopic crystallizations clogging the skin.[1]

In the process, direct current forms sodium hydroxide at the negative electrode, spreading across the outer skin and softening keratin so sebum plugs such as blackheads loosen. It does not destroy tissue as electrolysis does. Sessions typically last 10 to 15 minutes at about half to three milliamps, and are often followed by positive-electrode iontophoresis to apply water-soluble products and restore skin acidity.[1]

Iontophoresis, the broader method of moving charged molecules across skin with current, is established in medicine for conditions such as hyperhidrosis and sweat testing; its cosmetic application is described mainly in salon literature.[2]

chain: Negative electrode produces alkali on the skin
angle.text: Practitioners use it as a pre-extraction step to loosen congestion so the complexion looks smoother and clearer right after the facial.

paras: The negative electrode acts as the active applicator, in the form of a roller, ball, mask or cotton-wrapped tweezer electrode with a conductive solution. The alkali generated softens the outer layer and sebum plugs.[1] Reversing to the positive electrode helps reintroduce acidity and can deliver water-soluble ingredients.[1]
Desincrustation was developed by Societe P.A.B. in the early 1930s, building on 19th-century electrolysis principles and an earlier American device, the Electrolytic Cup.[1]

Treatment is typically folded into a facial before manual extraction. Retail listings describe machines combining desincrustation and iontophoresis, priced from around 170 pounds to about 500 dollars; these are vendor descriptions.
Spa-supply guidance cautions against galvanic desincrustation on inflamed acne, couperose skin or active pustules, and general electrotherapy cautions include implanted devices and pregnancy.
No studies found on cathiodermie machines for acne or pore appearance. Iontophoresis itself has been studied for medical uses such as hyperhidrosis.[2]

timeline.event: Societe P.A.B. develops desincrustation in France.[1]
